items.stem: Why should a class replication use a pilot study?
items.answer: To test materials and procedures and fix problems before collecting real data
items.markingKey: To test materials and procedures and fix problems before collecting real data. A pilot reveals unclear instructions, ceiling/floor effects or timing problems.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "If a replication finds a different result, the original study must have been fraudulent." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Different results may reflect sampling, cultural or procedural differences or chance; replication failures call for further research, not automatic accusations.
items.markingKey: Different results may reflect sampling, cultural or procedural differences or chance; replication failures call for further research, not automatic accusations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an aim and a hypothesis.
items.answer: An aim is a general statement of the purpose of the study; a hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about the operationalised variables.
items.markingKey: An aim is a general statement of the purpose of the study; a hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about the operationalised variables. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf is planning a class replication of Stroop (1935). The DV is time in seconds to name the ink colours of 20 words. Explain one way of controlling an extraneous variable in this replication.
items.answer: E.g. random allocation to conditions to spread participant variables, or counterbalancing in a repeated measures design to control order effects, or testing all participants at the same time of day in a quiet room.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant extraneous variable identified for this study; 1 mark: control described; 1 mark: explanation of how it protects internal validity.

items.stem: Briefly describe a ceiling effect in a pilot and explain what it reveals about the value of a pilot study.
items.answer: In a pilot of a word-recall replication in Vienna, almost every participant recalls all 10 words in both conditions. The task was too easy (ceiling effect), so differences could not appear; a longer list or shorter study time is needed before the main study
items.markingKey: Context (In a pilot of a word-recall replication in Vienna, almost every participant recalls all 10 words in both conditions.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the task was too easy (ceiling effect), so differences could not appear; a longer list or shorter study time is needed before the main study – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the value of a pilot study.

items.stem: Twenty volunteers in Kuala Lumpur complete a Stroop test twice: once while hearing recorded traffic noise through headphones and once in silence, a week apart, with the order counterbalanced. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
items.answer: IV: traffic noise vs silence during the task. DV: time in seconds to name the ink colours of 40 incongruent colour words.
items.markingKey: 1 mark IV: traffic noise vs silence during the task. 1 mark DV: time in seconds to name the ink colours of 40 incongruent colour words (must be operationalised, not just named).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Class replications of published studies are of little scientific value."
items.answer: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small, opportunity samples of peers; ethical constraints change procedures; demand characteristics. Arguments against: test reliability in a new cultural context; develop understanding of methods; can reveal limitations of original studies. Supported judgement: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings.

items.stem: Using two relevant studies, discuss the claim that class replications of published studies are of little scientific value.
items.answer: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings.
items.markingKey: For: small, opportunity samples of peers; ethical constraints change procedures; demand characteristics. Against: test reliability in a new cultural context; develop understanding of methods; can reveal limitations of original studies. Supported conclusion: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: Explain why a hypothesis must include operationalised variables.
items.answer: Only operationalised variables can be measured and tested; a hypothesis such as "music affects memory" cannot be shown to be true or false until "music" and "memory" are defined in measurable terms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Only operationalised variables can be measured and tested; a hypothesis such as "music affects memory" cannot be shown to be true or false until "music" and "memory" are defined in measurable terms. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A pilot study should be carried out before a class replication.
Reason (R): A pilot study allows problems with instructions, materials and timing to be fixed before real data are collected.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. R explains why pilots are recommended.

items.stem: Write standardised instructions for participants in a replication of the Stroop effect (no more than five sentences).
items.answer: E.g. "You will see a list of words printed in coloured ink. Name the colour of the ink, not the word, as quickly and accurately as you can. Start when I say go and stop at the last word. I will time you with a stopwatch. You may stop at any time."
items.markingKey: E.g. "You will see a list of words printed in coloured ink. Name the colour of the ink, not the word, as quickly and accurately as you can. Start when I say go and stop at the last word. I will time you with a stopwatch. You may stop at any time."

items.stem: Define the term "quantitative data".
items.answer: Numerical data that can be analysed statistically
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: numerical data that can be analysed statistically. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why raw data should be stored with participant codes rather than names.
items.answer: Codes protect confidentiality and anonymity while allowing the researcher to link each participant's scores across conditions and to delete data if a participant withdraws.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Codes protect confidentiality and anonymity while allowing the researcher to link each participant's scores across conditions and to delete data if a participant withdraws. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between quantitative data and qualitative data.
items.answer: Quantitative data are numerical and can be analysed statistically; qualitative data are descriptive (words, meanings) and are analysed thematically.
items.markingKey: Quantitative data are numerical and can be analysed statistically; qualitative data are descriptive (words, meanings) and are analysed thematically. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A study in Mumbai records number of aggressive acts observed. Identify the level of measurement and state the most appropriate measure of central tendency and of dispersion.
items.answer: Ratio data; central tendency: the mean; dispersion: the standard deviation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark level (ratio); 1 mark the mean; 1 mark the standard deviation. (Accept the median for interval/ratio data if outliers are mentioned.)

items.stem: Briefly describe a recall experiment with a scoring problem and explain what it reveals about organising and scoring data.
items.answer: In a class experiment in Bogotá, two students scored recall differently: one counted misspelled words as correct, the other did not. Without a clear operational scoring rule the data are unreliable; a coding rule must be agreed before scoring and applied to all participants
items.markingKey: Context (In a class experiment in Bogotá, two students scored recall differently: one counted misspelled words as correct, the other did not.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: without a clear operational scoring rule the data are unreliable; a coding rule must be agreed before scoring and applied to all participants – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to organising and scoring data.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Using the mean is always the best way to summarise data."
items.answer: The mean is best for interval/ratio data without extreme scores; otherwise the median or mode should be used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: uses all scores; basis for further statistics. Arguments against: distorted by outliers; inappropriate for nominal/ordinal data; may not be a real value. Supported judgement: The mean is best for interval/ratio data without extreme scores; otherwise the median or mode should be used.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A table that shows how often each value or category occurs"?
options: pilot study
range
frequency table
floor effect
items.answer: frequency table
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of frequency table.

items.stem: Sana writes: "A bar chart and a histogram are the same thing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A bar chart shows separate categories or condition means with gaps between bars; a histogram shows the distribution of continuous data with no gaps.
items.markingKey: A bar chart shows separate categories or condition means with gaps between bars; a histogram shows the distribution of continuous data with no gaps. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that using the mean is always the best way to summarise data.
items.answer: The mean is best for interval/ratio data without extreme scores; otherwise the median or mode should be used.
items.markingKey: For: uses all scores; basis for further statistics. Against: distorted by outliers; inappropriate for nominal/ordinal data; may not be a real value. Supported conclusion: The mean is best for interval/ratio data without extreme scores; otherwise the median or mode should be used. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The arithmetic average: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores"?
options: replication
raw data
mean
bar chart
items.answer: mean
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of mean.

items.stem: Distinguish between the mean and the median.
items.answer: The mean uses every score and is sensitive to outliers; the median is the middle value and is not affected by extreme scores.
items.markingKey: The mean uses every score and is sensitive to outliers; the median is the middle value and is not affected by extreme scores. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "If the mean of one condition is higher, the IV has definitely had an effect." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Descriptive statistics only describe the sample; an inferential test is needed to decide whether the difference is likely to be due to chance.
items.markingKey: Descriptive statistics only describe the sample; an inferential test is needed to decide whether the difference is likely to be due to chance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The raw data below show scores on a 30-item vocabulary test for 9 participants in a class practical: 19, 19, 19, 27, 19, 22, 26, 28, 13. State the mode.
items.answer: 19 marks
items.markingKey: A1: mode = 19 (the most frequent value, occurring 4 times).

items.stem: A student reports: "Condition A: mean 12, SD 1.2; Condition B: mean 12, SD 5.8." Interpret these results.
items.answer: The average performance is the same, but scores in B are much more spread out (less consistent); B may contain participants who were helped and others who were hindered by the condition.
items.markingKey: The average performance is the same, but scores in B are much more spread out (less consistent); B may contain participants who were helped and others who were hindered by the condition.

items.stem: Briefly describe a reaction-time experiment with one very slow participant and explain what it reveals about the choice of descriptive statistics.
items.answer: In a class experiment in Seoul, nine participants have reaction times between 300 and 420 ms but one took 1,900 ms because he was distracted. The outlier inflates the mean and SD; the median and range (or reporting the outlier and its cause) give a more accurate summary
items.markingKey: Context (In a class experiment in Seoul, nine participants have reaction times between 300 and 420 ms but one took 1,900 ms because he was distracted.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the outlier inflates the mean and SD; the median and range (or reporting the outlier and its cause) give a more accurate summary – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the choice of descriptive statistics.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Descriptive statistics are sufficient to draw conclusions from an experiment."
items.answer: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: summarise patterns clearly; show direction of effect and spread. Arguments against: cannot show whether differences are due to chance; can be distorted by outliers; do not show effect size relative to variability without further analysis. Supported judgement: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population.

items.stem: "Descriptive statistics are sufficient to draw conclusions from an experiment." Evaluate this claim with reference to research.
items.answer: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population.
items.markingKey: For: summarise patterns clearly; show direction of effect and spread. Against: cannot show whether differences are due to chance; can be distorted by outliers; do not show effect size relative to variability without further analysis. Supported conclusion: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population. items.stem: Explain why the standard deviation is usually better than the range.
items.answer: The range uses only two scores and is distorted by outliers, whereas the SD uses every score to show the average spread around the mean.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The range uses only two scores and is distorted by outliers, whereas the SD uses every score to show the average spread around the mean. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "If the mean of one condition is higher, the IV has definitely had an effect." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Descriptive statistics only describe the sample; an inferential test is needed to decide whether the difference is likely to be due to chance.
items.markingKey: Descriptive statistics only describe the sample; an inferential test is needed to decide whether the difference is likely to be due to chance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Sana tested the hypothesis that the number of aggressive acts recorded in a 10-minute playground observation would be higher after watching an aggressive cartoon than after watching a neutral cartoon.

Condition A (after watching an aggressive cartoon): 8, 4, 3, 1, 0, 10
Condition B (after watching a neutral cartoon): 12, 5, 7, 4, 4, 11

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 4.33, SD A = 3.93; mean B = 7.17, SD B = 3.54. The means are not in the predicted direction. Condition A has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 26/6 = 4.33, B = 43/6 = 7.17. A1 SD A = 3.93. A1 SD B = 3.54. R1 direction: does not support the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition A is more variable. R1 recognises that significance requires an inferential test.

items.stem: Which change would most increase the generalisability of a class experiment?
items.answer: Using a larger random sample from a wider population
items.markingKey: Using a larger random sample from a wider population. A larger, more representative sample improves population validity.

items.stem: A student claims: "A study with no ethical problems is automatically valid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ethics and validity are separate: a study can be ethical but poorly controlled, or valid but unethical.
items.markingKey: Ethics and validity are separate: a study can be ethical but poorly controlled, or valid but unethical. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a significant result in a class replication does not prove the original theory.
items.answer: A single small study can produce significant results by chance (type I error), samples are unrepresentative, and other explanations (demand characteristics, confounds) may account for the result. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single small study can produce significant results by chance (type I error), samples are unrepresentative, and other explanations (demand characteristics, confounds) may account for the result. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to a memory replication in a noisy hall, explain how it illustrates internal validity.
items.answer: In Accra, a group tested half their participants in a quiet library and half in a noisy hall because rooms were unavailable. Noise varied systematically with the conditions and became a confounding variable, so differences in recall cannot be attributed to the IV
items.markingKey: Context (In Accra, a group tested half their participants in a quiet library and half in a noisy hall because rooms were unavailable.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: noise varied systematically with the conditions and became a confounding variable, so differences in recall cannot be attributed to the IV – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to internal validity.

items.stem:
Kwame tested the hypothesis that the number of idea units recalled from a short passage would be higher when the title was given before reading than when no title was given.

Condition A (when the title was given before reading): 9, 7, 18, 11, 8, 3, 13
Condition B (when no title was given): 2, 10, 17, 8, 9, 12, 5

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 9.86, SD A = 4.78; mean B = 9.00, SD B = 4.83. The means are in the predicted direction. Condition B has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 69/7 = 9.86, B = 63/7 = 9.00. A1 SD A = 4.78. A1 SD B = 4.83. R1 direction: supports the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition B is more variable. R1 recognises that significance requires an inferential test.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The main limitation of class practicals is their sample."
items.answer: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small opportunity samples of peers; WEIRD, limited generalisability. Arguments against: procedural limitations (order effects, stopwatch timing); demand characteristics; ethical constraints. Supported judgement: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ceiling effect"?
options: When a task is so easy that most participants score near the maximum, hiding differences between conditions
A precise, testable prediction about the relationship between the operationalised IV and DV
The middle value when scores are placed in order
Data on a scale with equal intervals and a true zero, such as time or number of words recalled
items.answer: When a task is so easy that most participants score near the maximum, hiding differences between conditions
items.markingKey: A. "ceiling effect" is when a task is so easy that most participants score near the maximum, hiding differences between conditions.

items.stem: A correlational study found r = -0.45 between number of close friends and well-being score. Describe this correlation and explain why it cannot be used to conclude that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: A moderate negative correlation: as number of close friends increases, well-being score tends to decrease. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as socio-economic status could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (negative); 1 mark strength (moderate, r = -0.45); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. socio-economic status) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: With reference to the six concepts of the course, discuss the claim that the main limitation of class practicals is their sample.
items.answer: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important.
items.markingKey: For: small opportunity samples of peers; WEIRD, limited generalisability. Against: procedural limitations (order effects, stopwatch timing); demand characteristics; ethical constraints. Supported conclusion: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A small-scale trial run of a study to identify problems with materials or procedures before the main study"?
options: outlier
frequency table
materials
pilot study
items.answer: pilot study
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of pilot study.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "mean".
items.answer: The arithmetic average: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the arithmetic average: the sum of all scores divided by the number of scores. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Ratings of anxiety on a 1-10 scale are usually treated as which level of measurement?
items.answer: Ordinal
items.markingKey: Ordinal. Ratings can be ordered, but the gap between 3 and 4 may not equal the gap between 8 and 9.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a limitation of the sample and a limitation of the design.
items.answer: A design limitation concerns how the study was set up (e.g. order effects, lack of control); a sample limitation concerns who took part (e.g. size, representativeness).
items.markingKey: A design limitation concerns how the study was set up (e.g. order effects, lack of control); a sample limitation concerns who took part (e.g. size, representativeness). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Standardised instructions increase the reliability of an experiment.
Reason (R): Standardised instructions mean every participant receives the same information in the same way.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Consistency of procedure allows replication and reduces variation not caused by the IV.

items.stem: Explain why it is useful to report both a measure of central tendency and a measure of dispersion.
items.answer: Two conditions can have the same mean but very different spreads; dispersion shows how consistent the scores are and how representative the mean is.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two conditions can have the same mean but very different spreads; dispersion shows how consistent the scores are and how representative the mean is. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: What level of measurement is the number of words recalled from a list?
options: nominal
interval
ordinal
ratio
items.answer: ratio
items.markingKey: D. Equal intervals and a true zero.

items.stem: A correlational study found r = -0.64 between hours of revision and exam percentage. Describe this correlation and explain why it cannot be used to conclude that one variable causes the other.
items.answer: A moderate negative correlation: as hours of revision increases, exam percentage tends to decrease. Correlation does not establish causation; a third variable such as age could affect both, or causality could run in the opposite direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark direction (negative); 1 mark strength (moderate, r = -0.64); 1 mark causality: no IV is manipulated, so third variables (e.g. age) or bidirectional causality cannot be ruled out.

items.stem: Explain the difference between standardised instructions and a standardised procedure.
items.answer: Standardised instructions are the identical words given to all participants; a standardised procedure covers everything done in the study - instructions, materials, timing, order and setting.
items.markingKey: Standardised instructions are the identical words given to all participants; a standardised procedure covers everything done in the study - instructions, materials, timing, order and setting. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The raw data below show seconds taken to complete a jigsaw puzzle for 9 participants in a class practical: 119, 118, 51, 87, 97, 47, 165, 150, 82. Calculate the range and state what it shows.
items.markingKey: A1: range = 165 - 47 = 118. R1: it shows the spread between the highest and lowest score (but is distorted by extreme values).

items.stem: Rafael recorded the following frequencies: secure = 34; insecure-avoidant = 38; insecure-resistant = 9. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "insecure-avoidant" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 46.9%; modal category: insecure-avoidant
items.markingKey: A1 38/81 x 100 = 46.9%. A1 mode = insecure-avoidant (38).

items.stem: Suggest two modifications to a class Stroop replication that used 12 classmates and found no significant difference, and explain how each could improve the study.
items.answer: Larger and more varied sample (increases power and generalisability); counterbalance conditions to control order effects; use a longer word list to avoid floor/ceiling effects; time with software rather than stopwatches (more reliable).
items.markingKey: Larger and more varied sample (increases power and generalisability); counterbalance conditions to control order effects; use a longer word list to avoid floor/ceiling effects; time with software rather than stopwatches (more reliable).

items.stem: Chloé writes: "A pilot study is the same as the main study but with the results counted twice." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A pilot study is a small trial run whose purpose is to check materials and procedures; its data are not included in the main results.
items.markingKey: A pilot study is a small trial run whose purpose is to check materials and procedures; its data are not included in the main results. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A class in Cape Town predicted that the number of idea units recalled from a short passage would be greater when the title was given before reading than when no title was given.

Condition A (when the title was given before reading): 16, 11, 5, 13, 18, 5, 4
Condition B (when no title was given): 14, 6, 3, 8, 13, 5, 2

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 10.29, SD A = 5.71; mean B = 7.29, SD B = 4.68. The means are in the predicted direction. Condition A has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 72/7 = 10.29, B = 51/7 = 7.29. A1 SD A = 5.71. A1 SD B = 4.68. R1 direction: supports the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition A is more variable. R1 recognises that significance requires an inferential test.

items.stem: Construct a summary table for an experiment with two conditions (music vs silence) and 10 participants in each. State what should appear in the table and its title.
items.answer: Title stating IV and DV (e.g. "Mean and standard deviation of words recalled (out of 20) in the music and silence conditions"); rows/columns: condition, mean, SD (and n); units given.
items.markingKey: Title stating IV and DV (e.g. "Mean and standard deviation of words recalled (out of 20) in the music and silence conditions"); rows/columns: condition, mean, SD (and n); units given.

items.answer: Ethics and validity are separate: a study can be ethical but poorly controlled, or valid but unethical.

Supported conclusion: The mean is best for interval/ratio data without extreme scores; otherwise the median or mode should be used. Markbands (scaled to the marks available): top band - focused on the command term, accurate and detailed knowledge, research explicitly used as evidence, well-developed evaluation (methods, ethics, culture, alternative explanations) and a reasoned conclusion; middle band - mostly focused, relevant research partly linked, evaluation uneven; lower band - descriptive, research named but not used, little evaluation.

items.stem: "The main limitation of class practicals is their sample." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small opportunity samples of peers; WEIRD, limited generalisability. Arguments against: procedural limitations (order effects, stopwatch timing); demand characteristics; ethical constraints. Supported judgement: Sampling is a major limitation, but design and measurement issues are often equally important. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "pilot study".
items.answer: A small-scale trial run of a study to identify problems with materials or procedures before the main study
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a small-scale trial run of a study to identify problems with materials or procedures before the main study. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A large standard deviation indicates that:
options: Scores are widely spread around the mean
Most scores are close to the mean
There are no outliers
The mean is very high
items.answer: Scores are widely spread around the mean
items.markingKey: A. SD measures spread.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "frequency table"?
options: Non-numerical data such as words, descriptions or images
A table that shows how often each value or category occurs
Data in separate categories with no order, such as yes/no or attachment type
Repeating a published study using the same or very similar procedure to check whether its findings hold
items.answer: A table that shows how often each value or category occurs
items.markingKey: B. "frequency table" is a table that shows how often each value or category occurs.

items.stem: Explain why a significant result in a class replication does not prove the original theory.
items.answer: A single small study can produce significant results by chance (type I error), samples are unrepresentative, and other explanations (demand characteristics, confounds) may account for the result.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single small study can produce significant results by chance (type I error), samples are unrepresentative, and other explanations (demand characteristics, confounds) may account for the result. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a standardised procedure and standardised instructions.
items.answer: Standardised instructions are the identical words given to all participants; a standardised procedure covers everything done in the study - instructions, materials, timing, order and setting.
items.markingKey: Standardised instructions are the identical words given to all participants; a standardised procedure covers everything done in the study - instructions, materials, timing, order and setting. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the mean and the median.
items.answer: The mean uses every score and is sensitive to outliers; the median is the middle value and is not affected by extreme scores.
items.markingKey: The mean uses every score and is sensitive to outliers; the median is the middle value and is not affected by extreme scores. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between ordinal data and interval data.
items.answer: Ordinal data can be ranked but the gaps between values are not equal (e.g. Likert ratings); interval data have equal gaps between values (e.g. temperature in Celsius).
items.markingKey: Ordinal data can be ranked but the gaps between values are not equal (e.g. Likert ratings); interval data have equal gaps between values (e.g. temperature in Celsius). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a limitation of the design and a limitation of the sample.
items.answer: A design limitation concerns how the study was set up (e.g. order effects, lack of control); a sample limitation concerns who took part (e.g. size, representativeness).
items.markingKey: A design limitation concerns how the study was set up (e.g. order effects, lack of control); a sample limitation concerns who took part (e.g. size, representativeness). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "If a replication finds a different result, the original study must have been fraudulent." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Different results may reflect sampling, cultural or procedural differences or chance; replication failures call for further research, not automatic accusations.
items.markingKey: Different results may reflect sampling, cultural or procedural differences or chance; replication failures call for further research, not automatic accusations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an experiment carried out in Toronto, the number of schema-consistent items falsely "recalled" from an office scene were collected from 9 volunteers: 5, 5, 5, 8, 8, 6, 1, 2, 4. State the mode.
items.answer: 5 items
items.markingKey: A1: mode = 5 (the most frequent value, occurring 3 times).

items.stem: A study in Geneva records number of aggressive acts observed. Identify the level of measurement and state the most appropriate measure of central tendency and of dispersion.
items.answer: Ratio data; central tendency: the mean; dispersion: the standard deviation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark level (ratio); 1 mark the mean; 1 mark the standard deviation. (Accept the median for interval/ratio data if outliers are mentioned.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which a memory replication in a noisy hall shows internal validity.
items.answer: In Accra, a group tested half their participants in a quiet library and half in a noisy hall because rooms were unavailable. Noise varied systematically with the conditions and became a confounding variable, so differences in recall cannot be attributed to the IV
items.markingKey: Context (In Accra, a group tested half their participants in a quiet library and half in a noisy hall because rooms were unavailable.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: noise varied systematically with the conditions and became a confounding variable, so differences in recall cannot be attributed to the IV – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to internal validity.

items.stem: In Mexico City, students rate their mood (1-10) after 20 minutes of exercise and after 20 minutes of sitting, on two different days. Suggest one extraneous variable that could affect the results and explain how it could be controlled.
items.answer: Demand characteristics - participants may guess that exercise is expected to improve mood; use a cover story and a single-blind researcher.
items.markingKey: Demand characteristics - participants may guess that exercise is expected to improve mood; use a cover story and a single-blind researcher. 1 mark: plausible extraneous variable; 1 mark: why it could affect the DV; 1 mark: appropriate control (standardisation, random allocation, counterbalancing, matching).

items.stem: With reference to a reaction-time experiment with one very slow participant, explain how it illustrates the choice of descriptive statistics.
items.answer: In a class experiment in Seoul, nine participants have reaction times between 300 and 420 ms but one took 1,900 ms because he was distracted. The outlier inflates the mean and SD; the median and range (or reporting the outlier and its cause) give a more accurate summary
items.markingKey: Context (In a class experiment in Seoul, nine participants have reaction times between 300 and 420 ms but one took 1,900 ms because he was distracted.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the outlier inflates the mean and SD; the median and range (or reporting the outlier and its cause) give a more accurate summary – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the choice of descriptive statistics.

items.stem: Jonas recorded the following frequencies: secure = 32; insecure-avoidant = 37; insecure-resistant = 30. Calculate the percentage of the total that was "insecure-avoidant" (to 1 decimal place) and identify the modal category.
items.answer: 37.4%; modal category: insecure-avoidant
items.markingKey: A1 37/99 x 100 = 37.4%. A1 mode = insecure-avoidant (37).

items.stem:
Felix tested the hypothesis that ratings of trust (1-7) given to an unfamiliar partner in a trust game would be higher after a cooperative warm-up game than after a competitive warm-up game.

Condition A (after a cooperative warm-up game): 5, 7, 6, 4, 6, 6, 1
Condition B (after a competitive warm-up game): 3, 7, 5, 4, 6, 4, 1

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 5.00, SD A = 2.00; mean B = 4.29, SD B = 1.98. The means are in the predicted direction. Condition A has the larger SD, so its scores are more spread out (less consistent). Descriptive statistics alone cannot show that the difference is significant; an inferential test is needed.
items.markingKey: A1 means: A = 35/7 = 5.00, B = 30/7 = 4.29. A1 SD A = 2.00. A1 SD B = 1.98. R1 direction: supports the hypothesis. R1 spread: condition A is more variable. R1 recognises that significance requires an inferential test.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Class replications of published studies are of little scientific value."
items.answer: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small, opportunity samples of peers; ethical constraints change procedures; demand characteristics. Arguments against: test reliability in a new cultural context; develop understanding of methods; can reveal limitations of original studies. Supported judgement: Class replications are mainly educational, but well-designed ones can provide useful evidence about the reliability and generalisability of findings.

items.stem: "Descriptive statistics are sufficient to draw conclusions from an experiment." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: summarise patterns clearly; show direction of effect and spread. Arguments against: cannot show whether differences are due to chance; can be distorted by outliers; do not show effect size relative to variability without further analysis. Supported judgement: Descriptive statistics are essential for describing results, but inferential statistics are needed to draw conclusions about the population.
